items.prompt: A user adds an expense with the amount 12.345. What does the app print?
items.answer: "Could not add expense: Amount must use at most 2 decimal places."
distractors: "Added expense #1." with the amount rounded half-up to 12.35 on save
"Added expense #1." with the amount cut down to 12.34
"Could not add expense: Amount must be a valid number."
items.explanation: parseAmount calls setScale(2, RoundingMode.UNNECESSARY), which throws ArithmeticException when digits would have to be dropped; the catch turns that into the decimal-places message (reproduced). No rounding mode that changes the value is used, and 12.345 is a valid number.

items.prompt: A user adds an expense with the amount 12.340. What happens?
items.answer: It is added, and the amount is stored and shown as 12.34
distractors: It is refused, as the amount has three digits after the point
It is added, but the file keeps all three decimals, 12.340
It is refused, as amounts may not end with a trailing zero
items.explanation: setScale(2, UNNECESSARY) only throws when a non-zero digit would be lost. Dropping a trailing 0 does not change the value, so 12.340 becomes 12.34 (reproduced: the list and the file show 12.34).

items.prompt: A user types the category "  food   and DRINK " (extra spaces, mixed case). How is it stored?
items.answer: As Food And Drink, each word capitalised, with single spaces
distractors: As food and DRINK, with only the outer spaces trimmed away
As FOOD AND DRINK, since categories are always kept in upper case
As Food and drink, with only the very first letter capitalised
items.explanation: normalizeCategory trims, splits on runs of whitespace, upper-cases the first letter of each word and lower-cases the rest, then joins with single spaces (reproduced: the list shows Food And Drink).

items.prompt: In Add expense the user leaves the title blank, types abc as the amount, leaves the category blank and enters 2026-02-30. What happens?
items.answer: All five prompts are shown, then it reports "Title cannot be blank."
distractors: It stops at once after the empty title and asks for the title again
All five prompts are shown, then every one of the four errors is listed
All five prompts are shown, then it reports "Amount must be a valid number."
items.explanation: addExpenseFlow asks for all five values before calling addExpense, which validates title, amount, category and date in that order and throws at the first failure. Only the title error is printed (reproduced). Nothing re-prompts.

items.prompt: A user enters the date 2026-02-30 for a new expense. What message is printed?
items.answer: "Could not add expense: Date must use the format yyyy-MM-dd."
distractors: "Added expense #1." with the date rolled forward to 2026-03-02
"Added expense #1." with the date moved back to 2026-02-28
"Could not add expense: February 2026 only has 28 days in it."
items.explanation: LocalDate.parse rejects a day that does not exist with a DateTimeParseException, and parseDate maps every such exception to the same format message, even though the format here is fine (reproduced). LocalDate.parse never adjusts a date.

items.prompt: At "Month (yyyy-MM):" the user types 2026-3. What happens?
items.answer: It prints "Month must use the format yyyy-MM." and lists nothing
distractors: It lists every expense dated in March 2026, as 2026-3 means March
It prints "No expenses found." because no date is in month 2026-3
It lists every 2026 expense, as the month part is not understood
items.explanation: YearMonth.parse expects a two-digit month, so "2026-3" throws DateTimeParseException, which parseYearMonth turns into the format message and filterByMonthFlow prints (reproduced). No filtering happens at all.

items.prompt: expenses.txt has one expense in category transport (hand-typed, lowercase) and one in Transport. What does Show spending by category print for them?
items.answer: Two lines, transport $2.50 and Transport $4.00, totalled separately
distractors: One line, Transport $6.50, as categories are compared ignoring case
One line, transport $6.50, named after the first category it found
Two lines, both shown as Transport, $2.50 and $4.00, in file order
items.explanation: Categories are only normalised when typed in addExpense; loaded records keep the text from the file. getSpendingByCategory keys a LinkedHashMap by the exact category string, so the two spellings are separate keys (reproduced: "transport $2.50" and "Transport $4.00").

items.prompt: With the same two expenses (categories transport and Transport), the user filters by category and types TRANSPORT. What is listed?
items.answer: Both expenses, as the comparison ignores the letter case
distractors: Neither, as TRANSPORT matches no stored category exactly
Only the Transport one, as the input is normalised first
Only the transport one, as stored text is compared as is
items.explanation: getExpensesByCategory normalises the input to Transport and then compares with equalsIgnoreCase, which matches both spellings (reproduced). Normalising alone would match only Transport, but the case-insensitive comparison also takes transport.

items.prompt: expenses.txt has three expense lines, and the middle one has the amount x. What happens at start-up and after the user exits?
items.answer: It is skipped with a message, the rest load, and the next save drops it
distractors: Loading stops at it, so the app starts with an empty expense list
It is skipped with a message, and the save writes it back unchanged
It loads with an amount of 0.00, and the next save writes 0.00 for it too
items.explanation: load catches the IllegalArgumentException from parseLine per line, prints "Skipping invalid saved record on line N", and keeps going. The skipped line never reaches the manager, and the finally block in run() rewrites the file from the manager list, so the bad line is gone (reproduced).

items.prompt: expenses.txt holds valid expenses with ids 1 and 7. The user adds a new expense. Which id does it get?
items.answer: Id 8, as the next id is the highest loaded id plus one
distractors: Id 3, as the next id is the number of loaded expenses plus one
Id 2, as the lowest unused id is always chosen for the new one
Id 1, as ids are counted again from 1 every time the app starts
items.explanation: loadExpenses calls calculateNextId, which returns the highest id plus one; with 1 and 7 loaded that is 8, and the app prints "Added expense #8." (reproduced). Count and gaps are never used.

items.prompt: Someone hand-edits expenses.txt so an amount reads 2.505. The app starts and the user picks Show total spending. What happens?
items.answer: It loads, but option 5 crashes with an ArithmeticException
distractors: It is skipped at load time for using more than 2 decimals
It loads, and the total is rounded half-up and shown as $2.51
It loads, and the total is printed in full as $2.505
items.explanation: parseLine builds the BigDecimal and Expense directly, and neither checks the scale. formatAmount then calls setScale(2, RoundingMode.UNNECESSARY), which throws "Rounding necessary"; nothing catches it, so the program dies after the finally block saves (reproduced).

items.prompt: A user adds an expense and leaves the note empty, exits, and starts the app again. What happens to that expense?
items.answer: It is skipped at load for having 5 of 6 fields, and so it is lost
distractors: It loads normally, and the list shows a dash in the Note column there
It loads with its note set to the text null after a restart
It loads, but its date is then read from the empty note field instead
items.explanation: toLine ends the record with a tab and an empty note. load trims each line before parsing, which removes that trailing tab, so splitting gives 5 fields and the record is skipped; the next save then drops it (reproduced: "Skipping invalid saved record on line 2: Expected 6 fields but found 5."). This is a bug in the code; the README does not mention it.

items.front: What does it mean that Expense is immutable, and why is that useful here?
items.back: All fields are final and set once in the constructor, which also validates them, and there are no setters. Once an Expense exists it is valid and cannot change, so lists can share the same objects safely.

items.front: How does the storage keep a tab typed inside a title or note from splitting the record?
items.back: escape writes a backslash as \\ and a tab, newline or carriage return as \t, \n or \r. splitPreservingEscapes keeps a backslash and the character after it together, so only a raw tab separates fields; unescape then turns the codes back into the real characters.
So main can create it in a try-with-resources block. When run() returns, or throws, close() is called automatically and closes the Scanner, without a separate finally block in main.
